modules.title: What AI Does—and Does Not Do
modules.summary: Understand models as pattern-driven systems, not databases or people.
objectives: Explain the difference between a model and a search database.
Recognize why confident output can still be wrong.

sections.title: Models produce likely continuations
paragraphs: A language model learns patterns from large collections of examples. Given instructions and context, it generates a useful continuation one piece at a time.
That makes models excellent at explaining, transforming, drafting, classifying, and reasoning over supplied material. It does not make every output a stored fact.
sections.callout: Treat fluent language as a delivery style, not proof of correctness.

sections.title: Verification should match the stakes
paragraphs: Brainstorming can tolerate uncertainty. Medical, legal, financial, security, and production decisions require current authoritative evidence.
Good AI use combines a clear task, relevant context, constraints, and a way to verify the result.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a language model?
choices: A guaranteed database of current facts
A system that generates outputs from learned patterns and supplied context
A human expert stored inside software
questions.explanation: Models generate from patterns and context; fluent output is not a guarantee of factual accuracy.

choices: When the decision has high consequences
Only when the answer is short
Only when a model admits uncertainty
questions.explanation: Verification effort should increase with consequence, volatility, and uncertainty.

modules.title: Prompt with Purpose
modules.summary: Turn a vague request into a task an AI system can execute and you can evaluate.
objectives: Write prompts with a goal, context, constraints, and output contract.
Separate trusted instructions from untrusted input.

sections.title: A prompt is a working contract
paragraphs: Strong prompts say what outcome is needed, why it matters, what information is trustworthy, what boundaries apply, and what a successful response looks like.
The model should not have to guess the audience, format, source of truth, or definition of done.

code.label: Reusable prompt shape
code.code:
Goal: [OUTCOME]
Context: [TRUSTED FACTS]
Constraints: [BOUNDARIES]
Deliverable: [FORMAT]
Verify: [CHECKS]

sections.title: Inspect, correct, and reuse
paragraphs: Prompting is iterative. Inspect the result, identify the missing constraint or context, and improve the reusable instruction instead of repeatedly requesting a vague improvement.

questions.prompt: Which addition most improves an ambiguous request?
choices: A concrete outcome and acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: A testable outcome and acceptance criteria reduce guesswork and make evaluation possible.

questions.prompt: Why separate trusted context from untrusted content?
choices: To reduce instruction confusion and prompt-injection risk
questions.explanation: Clear trust boundaries help the system treat data as data rather than new instructions.

modules.title: Agents, Tools, and Guardrails
modules.summary: Understand what changes when a model can take actions.
objectives: Distinguish a chat response from an agentic loop.
Identify tool, permission, and verification boundaries.
Recognize when human approval is required.

sections.title: An agent observes, decides, acts, and checks
paragraphs: An agent combines a model with tools and a loop. It can inspect state, choose an action, use a tool, evaluate the result, and continue toward a goal.
Capability increases risk. Read access, file edits, messages, deployments, and destructive operations should have different permission and approval policies.

sections.title: Guardrails belong around the model
paragraphs: Reliable agent systems constrain tools, scope credentials, validate inputs and outputs, record actions, and stop for human decisions when consequences are difficult to reverse.
sections.callout: The model can recommend a safeguard; the surrounding system must enforce it.

questions.prompt: What makes an AI workflow agentic?
choices: It can choose and execute actions in a loop
questions.explanation: Agentic systems combine model decisions, tools, state, and repeated action toward a goal.

questions.prompt: Where should irreversible-action approval be enforced?
choices: In the surrounding tool and permission system
questions.explanation: Prompts guide behavior, but external controls enforce permissions and approval.

modules.title: Anthropic in Practice
modules.summary: Map Claude chat, API, and coding-agent workflows to the right job.
objectives: Separate conversational, API, and coding-agent use cases.
Choose context and tool boundaries deliberately.
Verify current model and product availability.

sections.title: One provider, several operating surfaces
paragraphs: Claude can be used through conversational products, APIs, and coding-agent tools. These surfaces differ in authentication, billing, context packaging, tools, and operational control.
Choose the surface from the workflow: interactive thinking, application integration, or repository execution.

sections.title: Treat model details as volatile
paragraphs: Model names, context limits, pricing, and regional availability change. Link to current official documentation instead of embedding long-lived routing rules without a verification date.

questions.prompt: What should drive the choice between chat, API, and coding agent?
choices: The workflow, control, and integration requirements
A single default for every task
questions.explanation: The operating surface should match how the work is performed and controlled.

questions.prompt: How should volatile model details be presented?
choices: With official sources and verification dates
questions.explanation: Source links and verification dates make changing claims auditable.

modules.title: OpenAI in Practice
modules.summary: Understand conversational, API, and Codex workflows without conflating them.
objectives: Separate ChatGPT, API, and Codex use cases.
Design around tools and structured outputs.
Verify current models and platform behavior.

sections.title: Match the product surface to the job
paragraphs: Conversational products support direct knowledge work, APIs integrate model behavior into software, and coding agents work across repositories and development tools.
Authentication, data controls, billing, and tool availability vary across these surfaces.

sections.title: Applications need contracts
paragraphs: When software consumes model output, use structured contracts, validation, retries, and observable failure behavior instead of parsing unconstrained prose.

questions.prompt: What is the safest way for software to consume model output?
choices: Use a structured contract and validate it
Assume every response has the same shape
questions.explanation: Structured, validated output creates an explicit application boundary.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish ChatGPT, API, and Codex workflows?
choices: They have different operating and control models
questions.explanation: The surfaces differ in interaction, integration, permissions, and operations.

modules.title: Choose a Provider Deliberately
modules.summary: Use requirements and evaluation evidence instead of loyalty or a static leaderboard.
objectives: Include security, data, cost, and operational requirements.
Use different model families when independent review matters.

sections.title: Start from the work
paragraphs: Evaluate providers against representative tasks, quality rubrics, latency, total cost, context needs, tool support, data controls, deployment requirements, and team operations.
A provider can be best for one workflow and a poor fit for another.

sections.title: Independence can improve review
paragraphs: For important review, a different model family can reduce correlated blind spots. Independence does not replace tests or expert judgment, but it adds a useful perspective.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest provider-selection method?
questions.explanation: Representative tasks and operational constraints measure fit for the actual workflow.

questions.prompt: Why use a different model family for important review?
questions.explanation: Cross-family review adds independence but still requires objective checks.

resources.title: AI Glossary
resources.summary: Plain-language definitions for models, prompts, context, agents, tools, retrieval, and evaluations.

sections.title: Core terms
paragraphs: Model: a system that generates or evaluates outputs from learned patterns and current input.
Prompt: instructions and context supplied to a model.
Context window: the limited working material available for one interaction.
Agent: a model-driven system that can select tools and act in a loop.
Evaluation: a repeatable method for measuring output against explicit criteria.

resources.title: Prompt Checklist
resources.summary: A compact preflight for tasks, context, constraints, output, and verification.

sections.title: Before you send
paragraphs: State the outcome and audience.
Supply the trusted context and source of truth.
Name constraints, exclusions, and permissions.
Specify the output format.
Define how the result will be checked.

resources.title: Agent Safety Checklist
resources.summary: Permission, data, verification, logging, and rollback questions before an agent acts.

sections.title: Before granting tools
paragraphs: Limit tools and credentials to the task.
Separate read, reversible write, external communication, and destructive permissions.
Validate untrusted input and tool output.
Record material actions.
Require human approval and rollback for high-consequence changes.

resources.title: Provider Decision Card
resources.summary: A reusable comparison card for quality, cost, data, tools, and operations.

sections.title: Score the actual workflow
paragraphs: Representative task quality and failure modes.
Latency, throughput, and total cost.
Context, tool use, and structured output.
Data handling, identity, region, and compliance.
SDK, observability, support, and team familiarity.
